en: The Guru-gītā in its Extended Form. Chapter One.
Salutation to Brahman, whose form is inconceivable and unmanifest, who is devoid of qualities yet is the soul of all hosts, and whose form is the support of the entire universe. 1.

Salutations to that Brahman which is inconceivable, unmanifest, and devoid of the three qualities (yet, through the limiting adjunct of the ignorance of perceivers, appears as consisting of the three qualities and as the substratum of the entire universe).
The Sages said:
O Sūta, O Sūta, O you of great wisdom, who have reached the further shore of the Nigamas and Āgamas!
Tell us the true nature of the Guru, which removes all impurities.
The sages said:

O possessor of great wisdom, O you who are well-versed in the Vedas and Vedāṅgas! Dear Sūtajī, describe to us the true nature of the Guru, which destroys all sins and by the mere hearing of which an embodied being is liberated from suffering.
By which path the sages attained omniscience.
"By the mere hearing of which a person is liberated from suffering, and by which means the sages attained omniscience—
that supreme reality, reaching which a man never again enters the bondage of saṃsāra— must now be explained by you. (4)
Please describe that supreme reality, attaining which a person is no longer bound by the fetters of worldly existence.
O Sūta, tell us all of that—the essence of the *Gurugītā*, which is especially the most secret of secrets—since it is to be heard through your grace. (5)

"That reality which is supremely mystical, most excellent, and the very essence—especially the Guru-Gītā—we wish to hear through your grace, O dear Sūtajī! Please narrate it to us. Thus was Sūta repeatedly entreated by the assembly of sages.
With great curiosity, he spoke these sweet words.
Sūta said:
Listen, all you sages, with supreme faith and joy;
I shall speak the Gītā, which is the nature of a mother and destroys the disease of worldly existence. 7.
Formerly, on the peak of Kailāsa, frequented by Siddhas and Gandharvas,
there stood an exceedingly beautiful palace made of the flowers of the Kalpa-vines.
In one place, he was seated upon a tiger skin, surrounded by a host of sages, being praised by Śuka and other seers, as he was awakening them to the supreme reality.
Seeing him constantly bowing his face and paying homage with devotion, Pārvatī was filled with wonder and questioned him. 10.
Pārvatī said:
Oṃ! Salutations, O God, Lord of gods, Supreme beyond the supreme, Teacher of the world!
Gods, asuras, and humans always pay homage to you with devotion. (11)
"You are indeed always to be worshipped by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Mahendra, and the others;
to whom then do you pay homage, you who are yourself the very locus of prostration? (12)
Having seen this vast and wonderful deed, it appears miraculous to me.
What is this? I do not understand; tell me out of compassion, O Lord! (13)
O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, leader of vows, O Śambhu, please out of compassion tell me of the supreme majesty of the Guru, the foremost among all observances. 14.
"O Lord, by what path may a living being become composed of Brahman?
O Master, have mercy on me; I bow at your feet. (15)
Thus repeatedly entreated, Mahādeva Maheśvara,
with his heart filled with the weight of bliss, spoke this to Pārvatī.
Śrī Mahādeva said:
"O Goddess, this must not be spoken; it is a secret, the most profound of secrets.
It was never told to anyone before, yet for the sake of your devotion, I shall speak of it. (17)
"O Goddess, you are my very form; therefore, I shall tell it to you. This question, which benefits the world, has never been asked by anyone before. (18)
For that high-souled one who possesses supreme devotion to the Divine, and whose devotion to the teacher is equal to that toward the Divine—verily, these truths declared here shine forth for him. 19.
He who is the Guru is declared to be Śiva; he who is Śiva is remembered as the Guru.
He who makes a distinction between them is a man who has violated the bed of his teacher.
That which is difficult to find in the three worlds, listen as I declare it:
there is no one other than the Guru and Brahman, truly, truly, O fair-faced one. 21.
The Vedas, the Shastras, the Puranas, and histories such as these, as well as the sciences of mantras and yantras, including the rites of delusion, eradication, and so forth; ||22||
For the Śaiva and Śākta Āgamas and many other doctrines are indeed corruptions for all living beings whose minds are deluded. (23)
O beloved, recitation, austerity, vows, pilgrimage, sacrifice, and likewise charity—all these become useless if the true nature of the Guru is not understood. 24.
O fair-faced one, there is no truth other than the Guru who is one's own Self; this is the truth, the truth.
Therefore, wise men should exert effort for the sake of attaining Him. 25.
Concealed ignorance is the illusion of the world, and the body arises from nescience;
that wisdom by whose grace it is described by the word "Guru" [is this very wisdom]. (26)
I bow down to that Guru, whose pair of lotus feet wards off the suffering of duality and serves as the means of crossing the ocean of worldly existence. 27.
Since an embodied being may become Brahman, I shall speak for the sake of your grace:
through service to the feet of the Śrī Guru, one's self becomes purified of all sins. (28)
By drinking the water from the feet of the Guru and holding the remainder upon his head, a man obtains the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords. 29.
The water from the feet of the Guru thoroughly dries up the mire of sin, kindles the brilliance of wisdom, and truly enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra. (30)
One should drink the water from the feet of the Guru for the sake of attaining knowledge and realized wisdom—that which uproots the foundation of ignorance and wards off rebirth and karma. (31)
Drinking the water from the guru’s feet, eating the remnants of the guru’s food, constant meditation upon the form of the guru, and the perpetual chanting of the guru’s name. ||32||
The chanting of one's own teacher’s name is the chanting of the infinite Śiva;
the contemplation of one's own teacher’s name is the contemplation of the infinite Śiva. (33)
We worship that Lord and Teacher, the dust of whose feet constantly serves as a bridge for someone in the ocean of worldly existence. 34.
Salutations be to that Supreme Soul, the illustrious Lord of Teachers, by whose mere grace both sorrow and delusion perish. 35.
Salutations to that illustrious Lord of Teachers, by receiving whose grace one may cast off great ignorance; may he grant the attainment of our desired goals. 36.

The sacred field of Kāśī is my dwelling, the water from the feet of the Gaṅgā is my drink, the Lord of the Universe (Viśveśvara) is my manifest Guru, and the realization of Brahman is my liberation. ||37||
Service to the guru is said to be Gayā; the body becomes the imperishable banyan tree (Vaṭa).
His feet are the feet of Viṣṇu; what is given there is infinite. ||38||
One should constantly meditate on the form of the Guru, always chant the name of the Guru, carry out the command of the Guru, and never conceive of anyone other than the Guru. 39.
Brahman, which resides within the mouth of the Guru, is attained through his grace;
one should always meditate upon the Guru, just as a woman of noble family meditates upon her own husband. 40.
Having abandoned his own hermitage, his own caste, his own fame, and that which increases his prosperity—all of this—he should take refuge in the teacher alone. (41)
Those who, thinking of nothing else, contemplate that supreme bliss which is easily attained;
therefore, with every effort, perform the service of the Guru. 42.
The Vidyā resides in the mouth of the Guru and is obtained through devotion to the Guru;
in the three worlds, the gods, sages, ancestors, and humans are the clear proclaimers [of this]. 43.
The syllable *gu* is indeed darkness, while the syllable *ru* is said to be light;
the Guru alone is Brahman, which devours ignorance—of this there is no doubt. (44)
The syllable *gu* signifies the disease of existence (*bhavaroga*), while the syllable *ru* is that which brings about its cessation;
because he removes the disease of existence, he is called *Guru*. 45.
The syllable *gu* transcends qualities (*guṇa*) and transcends form (*rūpa*); the syllable *ru* likewise transcends them. Because it is devoid of both quality and form, it is designated as *guru*.
The letter *gu* is the first syllable, which illuminates the qualities such as Māyā;
the letter *ru* is the Supreme Brahman, which brings liberation from the delusion of Māyā. (47)
Thus, the state of the Guru is supreme, difficult to attain even for the gods, and is worshipped by Garuḍas, Uragas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and other deities. (48)
"O Dhruva, grant [this] to those seeking liberation; there is no reality higher than the Guru.
One should perform service to the Guru and offer up one's own life. (49)
The practitioner should provide a seat, a bed, clothing, a vehicle, ornaments, and so forth, as a means to bring satisfaction to the Guru. ||50||
One should always propitiate the guru through action, mind, and speech;
having bowed with arms extended like long staffs, they remained free from shame in the presence of their guru. (51)
One should offer to the true gurus everything—body, senses, vital breath, wealth, one's own kin and relatives, wife, and so forth. (52)
The Guru alone is the entire universe, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
there is nothing higher than the Guru, therefore one should worship the Guru. 53.
Therefore, one should worship the Guru, whose lotus feet are resplendent with the jewels that are the crest-jewels of all the Vedas, and who is the expounder of the meaning of the Vedānta. 54.
He from whose mere remembrance knowledge arises spontaneously is himself all prosperity; therefore, one should worship the guru. 55.
O fair-faced one, know that this body is infested by millions of worms, defiled by a multitude of foul odors, impermanent, and an abode of suffering. (56)
Salutations to that illustrious Guru who rescues all those who, having climbed the tree of saṃsāra, fall into the ocean of hell. ||57||
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman—salutations to that venerable Guru. 58.
Salutations to that illustrious Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance has been opened with the collyrium-stick of knowledge. 59.
Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed—the state which is of the form of an unbroken circle and by which all that is moving and unmoving is pervaded. 60.
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom the "thou" (tvaṃpada) has been revealed as pervading all that is stationary and moving, everything that is animate and inanimate. 61.

Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom the entire triple world, including all moving and non-moving beings, has been pervaded as consisting of consciousness, and by whom his own state of being the Unstruck Sound (anāhata) has been revealed. 62.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whose word one is liberated from bondage in the mere twinkling of an eye, having beheld one's own self as Śiva. 63.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, who is consciousness, eternal, peaceful, beyond the ether, stainless, and transcendent of sound, the point, and the creative energy.
Salutation to that venerable Guru who is devoid of qualities, stainless, peaceful, both moving and stationary, and by whom the entire universe is pervaded. 65.
He is my father, he is my mother, he is my kinsman, and he is my deity;
salutations to that illustrious Guru for the destruction of the delusion of saṃsāra. ||66||
Salutation to that venerable Guru, by whose existence the world is real, by whose light it shines, and by whose bliss beings rejoice. 67.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, in whom all this is established and who shines as the very form of its manifestation; he who is the beloved of sons and others through his affection. 68.
Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom this reality—namely the mind, its mental factors, and so forth, as well as the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—has been thus revealed. (69)
Salutation to that venerable Guru, whose knowledge is this universe, which is not perceived as consisting of diverse distinctions, and who is eternally of a single, uniform nature. (70)
Salutations to that venerable Guru, whose thought is known by him who knows, but who is not known by him who does not know, and who exists in a state of non-dual being. 71.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, who, though being the nature of the cause, appears in the form of the effect; salutations to him whose very nature is both cause and effect. ||72||
This universe appears in manifold forms, yet no duality exists therein;
salutations to that venerable Guru, who is the very nature of cause and effect. ||73||
Salutations to that venerable Guru, who is adorned with the garland of principles mounted upon the power of knowledge, and who bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 74.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by the power of whose wind of knowledge the bonds of karma accumulated over many births are consumed. 75.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, whose water from the feet of the teacher dries up the ocean of worldly existence and kindles the wealth of the nectar of immortality. 76.
There is no reality greater than the Guru; there is no austerity greater than the Guru;
there is no knowledge greater than the Guru. Homage to that illustrious Guru! 77.
The Lord of Men, Śrī Jagannātha, my Guru, the illustrious Teacher of the World, who is my own self and the self of all beings—to that Śrī Guru, I offer salutation. ||78||
The Guru is the beginning and is without beginning; the Guru is the supreme deity.
There is nothing equal to the mantra of the Guru. Salutations to that illustrious Guru. (79)
When adversity has arisen, the teacher who embodies all righteousness is the one supreme kinsman; homage to that illustrious Guru! (80)
The universe resides within the Guru, and the Guru resides within the universe;
the Guru is the universe and there is nothing else—salutation to that illustrious Guru. 81.
Salutations to that venerable Guru who has shown the path to one who has entered the forest of existence with a mind bewildered by the confusion of directions. (82)
Salutations to that venerable Guru, whose water from the feet is the Gaṅgā for those living beings on earth whose names have not been pacified by the fires of the three-fold suffering. 83.
For living beings bitten by the serpent of ignorance, who is there a physician other than the true Guru, who knows the great mantra of perfect knowledge? 84.
Salutations to the Guru, who is the cause of the worlds, the bridge across the ocean of saṃsāra, the source of all sciences, and Śambhu himself. 85.
The root of meditation is the form of the Guru; the root of worship is the feet of the Guru;
the root of mantra is the word of the Guru; the root of liberation is the grace of the Guru. 86.
Whatever fruit is obtained from bathing at all the sacred fords as far as the seven oceans,
that fruit is not equal to even a thousandth part of a drop of water from the feet of the Guru.
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all.
Having properly obtained a Kula-guru, one should take refuge in that very Guru alone. 88.
Just as a bee, greedy for honey, goes from flower to another flower, so too a disciple, greedy for knowledge, should go from teacher to another teacher. (89)
I bow to the pair of the Guru’s feet, which transcend the sphere of speech and mind, distinguished by white and red radiance, and consisting of the essence of Śiva and Śakti. 90.

He who bestows the syllable *gu*, which transcends the qualities (*guṇa*), and the syllable *rū*, which is devoid of form—indeed, he who gives that which is beyond qualities and form—is known as a Guru. ||91||
Śiva is known as the three-eyed one, and Hari is remembered as having two arms;
he who is the four-faced Brahmā is declared to be the Śrī Guru, O beloved. (92)
I join my palms in reverence for the sake of attaining the state of an ocean of compassion, by whose grace a living being becomes liberated from the manifold cycle of existence. (93)
Those of meager fortune do not behold the supreme form of the illustrious Guru before them with the eye of discernment, just as the blind do not see the rising of the sun. (94)
At that very moment, he becomes the savior of families and tens of millions of families;
therefore, recognizing him as the true guru, one should salute him at the three times of day. 95.
O beloved, one should daily offer salutations with devotion toward that direction in which the pair of feet of Śrīnātha shines. 96.
One should constantly worship the Guru, praising him with prostrations made with all eight limbs; through such worship, one attains stability and becomes identical with one's own true nature. ||97||
With the two hands, the two feet, the two knees, the chest, the head, the eyes, the mind, and speech—this is called the eight-limbed prostration (aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma). ||98||
Let this [offering] be constantly cast toward that direction with sweet-sounding flowers,
for there the Blessed One, the sovereign of teachers, remains ever awake.
The eternal witness of the drama of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the universe. ||99||

What need is there for those [practices] that are not free from fear, which require a long time to purify, which bestow disease, which are difficult to perform, which involve many physical efforts, and which are painful and hard to endure—
[that practice] by the rising of which the powerful vital wind itself perishes in that very instant?
To attain that innate nature, one should constantly attend upon a single guru. ||100||
Without knowledge, the state of liberation is attained through devotion to the Guru;
for those who follow the path of the Guru, there is no other means than the grace of the Guru. 101.
Since there is nothing higher than this, as the Śruti declares "not this, not this," one should propitiate the Guru with truth through both mind and speech. 102.
By the grace and favor of the Guru, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, and all others attained the capacity for the tasks of creation, preservation, and dissolution. 103.
Neither the gods, kinnaras, gandharvas, nor the ancestors and yakṣas, nor even Tumburu and the sages, know the proper method for serving one's preceptor. ||104||
O beloved, the logicians, the Vedic scholars, the astrologers, the ritualists, and the worldly people do not know the untroubled reality of the Guru. 105.
Then, through the pride of great egoism and by the power of ignorance, they wander again in this cycle of existence like a waterwheel. (106)
Even those who perform sacrifices are not liberated, nor are the practitioners of yoga; even ascetics are not liberated if they are turned away from the true nature of the Guru. (107)
The Gandharvas, Pitṛs, Yakṣas, Cāraṇas, Ṛṣis, Siddhas, gods, and others who are averse to service toward their gurus are not liberated. ||108||
Thus ends the first chapter of the Śrī Gurugītā, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara, within the Uttara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
The Gurusong in its Extended Form.
Now begins the second chapter.
Listen, O Great Goddess, to the description of meditation, which bestows all bliss, brings about all happiness, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 109.
I remember the glorious Supreme Brahman, the Guru; I worship the glorious Supreme Brahman, the Guru;
I speak of the glorious Supreme Brahman, the Guru; I bow to the glorious Supreme Brahman, the Guru. 110.

The bliss of Brahman, which bestows supreme happiness, the embodiment of absolute knowledge, transcending all duality, resembling the sky, the goal indicated by "That thou art" and other great sayings—
unique, eternal, stainless, immovable, and the witness of all cognitions.
I bow to that true Guru, who has transcended all states of being and is devoid of the three qualities (guṇas). ||111||

One should meditate upon the Guru, whose divine form is seated upon a lion-throne situated in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus; who shines with the radiance of the crescent moon, and who bestows the desired boons of existence, consciousness, and bliss. 112.
Clad in white garments, adorned with white unguents and flowers, decorated with pearls, joyful, and two-eyed;
with his divine Śakti seated upon his left lap, possessing a gentle smile, he is a treasury of perfect compassion. ||113||

I perpetually bow to the illustrious Guru, whose nature is pure consciousness, who is endowed with his own innate being, who is bliss itself and the bestower of bliss, who is serene, the lord of yogis worthy of praise, and the physician for the disease of worldly existence. 114.

I bow to the lotus feet of the gurus, who have revealed the ocean of the bliss of one's own self; for people, those feet serve as a mere pill to pacify the delusion of the world’s hālāhala poison. 115.
One should worship that Guru in whom the fivefold activity—consisting of creation, maintenance, dissolution, restraint, and grace—is eternally manifest. (116)
Within his own lotus-feet, he perceives the all-consuming forest fire of saṃsāra as the fire of time (Kālānala);
and within the lotus situated at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), he perceives the lunar disc.

One should meditate upon the Guru situated in the center of the thousand-petaled mandala within the lotus of the three lines of the *akathādi* [vowels], and within the triangle on the side of the *haṃsa*. 118.
I bow to the Guru, who is Brahman—eternal, pure, free from appearance, formless, untainted, eternally awakened, and the bliss of consciousness. 119.
The creator of the entire universe, the one who has fashioned all created things,
the vision of all the Vedas, the sole creator of the reality of the existent;
the supreme lord beyond those attributes, whose vision is fixed solely upon the reality of the existent.
He is the supreme lord of existence and its qualities, whose sole vision is fixed upon the path to liberation. ||120||
The pillar that establishes the stage of the entire world,
the rain of the aesthetic sentiment of compassion, the synthesis of the garland of principles,
the creator of all conventions, and the vision of being, consciousness, and bliss.
May the divine vision of the venerable Guru dwell within me eternally. ||121||
Nothing is superior to the Guru, nothing is superior to the Guru, nothing is superior to the Guru, nothing is superior to the Guru;
according to the teaching of Śiva, according to the teaching of Śiva, according to the teaching of Śiva, according to the teaching of Śiva. 122.
This alone is auspicious, this alone is auspicious; this alone is auspicious, this alone is auspicious.
By the command of Hari, by the command of Hari, by the command of Hari, by the command of Hari. (123)
Known, known, known, known; secluded, secluded, secluded, secluded;
by the decree of fate, by the decree of fate, by the decree of fate, by the decree of fate. (124)
Having meditated upon the Guru in this manner, knowledge arises spontaneously;
then, by the Guru’s instruction, one should contemplate: "I am liberated. (125)
One should effect purification of the mind by the path taught by the guru;
one should break down everything perceived as "self" as being impermanent. 126.
All that is to be known is perceived, and knowledge is called the mind;
one should make knowledge and the object of knowledge equal—there is no other second path. 127.
What is the use of much speaking here, even with hundreds of millions of treatises?
Resting of the mind is difficult to attain without the supreme grace of the Guru. 128.
Having severed the eightfold fetters of the disciple with the stroke of the sword of compassion, he who perfectly generates true bliss is called a true guru. 129.
Having heard this, O Great Goddess, he who reviles his guru goes to terrible hells for as long as the moon and sun endure. (130)
O Goddess, as long as the body lasts until the end of the kalpa, one should remember the Guru; one must not neglect the Guru, even if one should become independent. 131.
Wise disciples should never utter the sound "huṃ";
nor should they ever speak untruth in the presence of the guru. ||132||
One who addresses a guru with "thou" or "hum," or speaks in the presence of the guru in such a manner, will become a Brahmarākṣasa in a waterless forest region. ||133||
One should constantly contemplate non-duality at all times and in all conditions; one should never entertain the notion of duality in the presence of the Guru. (134)
One should perform the worship of the Guru's feet until the point of forgetting the visible world;
for such a person alone is there liberation, and not for anyone other than him. 135.
Even if one who knows the complete reality should abandon the Guru, intense distraction indeed arises for him at the time of death. (136)

One should not neglect the teacher’s work, nor should one perform any task without having asked for permission. Indeed, adorned by the very presence of the teacher, one should not rise from one's seat without having saluted him. 137.
O Goddess, while a guru is present, one should never give instruction to others oneself; if one does so, one would become a rākṣasa.
One should not engage in difficult drinking or wandering about in the hermitage of the guru;
one should not exercise authority over initiation, exposition, and so forth, without having obtained the guru's permission. 139.
One should not occupy a hermitage bed, nor stretch out one's feet, nor engage in bodily luxuries and the like, nor even any other kind of playfulness. (140)
One should not transgress whatever has been spoken by the gurus, whether it be good or bad;
carrying out their command day and night, one should dwell with the guru like a servant. 141.
One should never enjoy the property of a guru without it being given;
even when it is given, it should be accepted like a pauper, for by this means even one's life is preserved. 142.
Whatever sandals, seats, beds, or other items are favored by the Guru, one should pay homage to them all; one should never touch them with one's feet. 143.
One should walk behind those who are walking; one should not step over the shadow of the guru.
One should not wear ostentatious dress, nor ornaments that are excessively showy. (144)
Upon seeing one who reviles the guru, one should drive him away or banish him; or else, that place itself should be abandoned if [the offender] is incapable of having his tongue cut out. 145.
One should not give one's leftovers to anyone, nor should one disregard the command of the guru;
having taken all the leftovers, one should consume them oneself like an oblation. 146.
One should not speak what is false, nor what is unpleasant, nor with pride, nor excessively;
one should not speak as if constrained by a command, but should manifest the teacher's authority.
"O Lord! O Master of the lords of the gods! O Sovereign! O King! O Lord of the family!"—frightened by such addresses, one should conduct oneself in the presence of the Guru. (148)
O Pārvatī, whether one has been cursed by sages, serpents, or even gods, or if one fears death at the appointed time, the Guru protects such a person.
For even the gods and others are powerless, and likewise the sages are powerless to protect one who has been struck by a preceptor’s curse anywhere at all. ||150||
O Goddess, this king of mantras consists of the two syllables "gu-ru";
it is undoubtedly the very essence of the Smṛtis, Vedas, and Purāṇas. 151.
One who carries a staff and a water-pot for the sake of receiving hospitality, honor, and worship is not to be called a renunciant; a true renunciant is one who is devoted solely to knowledge. 152.
Those who understand the Great Saying through service at the feet of the Guru are indeed called renunciants; others are merely wearers of the outward garb. 153.
He who directly realizes in this world the eternal Brahman—formless, devoid of qualities, and a mass of truth and consciousness—his status as a guru truly shines. 154.
Through the grace of the Guru and by beholding the Self within one's own self as the one who delights in the Self, self-knowledge proceeds by way of equanimity on the path to liberation. 155.
I bow to that which consists of the universe—the nature of the Supreme Self extending from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—comprising both the stationary and the moving. 156.
I bow to the Teacher of the World, who is existence-consciousness-bliss, beyond all mental constructs, eternal, perfect, formless, devoid of qualities, and established in his own self. 157.
One should constantly meditate upon that which is higher than the highest, the source of bliss, situated in the center of the space of the heart, resembling pure crystal. 158.
Just as the form of crystal appears in a crystal and the reflection of a mirror in a mirror, so too does the blissful form of consciousness appear within the Self as "I am He. (159)
One should meditate upon the Person, who consists of consciousness, as the size of a thumb within the heart;
hear now from me that state which flashes forth therein. 160.
I am unborn and I am immortal; indeed, I am without beginning or end.
I am changeless, consciousness-bliss, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great. 161.
It is without prior or posterior, eternal, self-luminous, and free from affliction;
it is the stainless supreme ether, fixed, blissful, and imperishable. ||162||
O Pārvatī, one should know that Brahman is by its very nature beyond the range of the senses, unapproachable, devoid of name and form, and silent. 163.
Just as the nature of fragrance exists in camphor, flowers, and the like, so too does the eternal nature of coldness and heat exist in Brahman. 164.
Just as earrings, bracelets, and other ornaments exist by their own nature as gold, so too am I the eternal Brahman. 165.
Having become oneself such as that, one should remain wherever one may be; through meditation, one becomes like a bee following a worm. 166.
Having thus performed meditation on the Guru, one becomes oneself composed of Brahman;
liberated in the body, in the word, and likewise in form, there is no doubt in this matter. 167.
Śrī Pārvatī said: O Mahādeva, what indeed is the *piṇḍa*, and what is declared to be the *pada*?
What is formless, and what is form? Tell me this, O Śaṅkara. (168)
Śrī Mahādeva said:
The *piṇḍa* is the power Kuṇḍalinī; the *pada* is declared to be Haṃsa;
the *rūpa* is to be known as Bindu; and that which transcends form is Nirañjana. 169.

O fair-faced one, those who are liberated in the aggregate (piṇḍa), liberated in the word (pada), and liberated in form (rūpa)—those who are liberated in that which transcends form (rūpātīta) are truly liberated; of this there is no doubt. ||170||
By means of meditation alone, the embodied soul becomes eternally one with Brahman;
wherever he may abide, he is liberated—of this there is no doubt. (171)
O beloved, the Blessed Śrī Guru is indeed endowed with the six qualities: knowledge, self-realization, tranquility, dispassion, eloquence, and fortitude, as well as sovereign power. 172.
The Guru is Śiva; the Guru is the God; the Guru is the kinsman of all embodied beings.
The Guru is the Self; the Guru is the life-force; nothing exists apart from the Guru. 173.
He who shines with the nature of a child—solitary, free from desire, peaceful, and devoid of anxiety, envy, and the like—is called a knower of Brahman. 174.
There is no happiness in the Vedas or the Shastras, nor is there happiness in mantras and yantras;
apart from the grace of the Guru, there is no happiness on this earth. 175.
In the systems of the Cārvākas and Vaiṣṇavas there is no happiness, nor indeed in the Prābhākara school;
that which is approved by Vedānta is the happiness found at the feet of the Guru. (176)
Neither the happiness of the lord of the gods nor the happiness of universal monarchs is equal to the happiness of the sage who is free from passion and dwells in solitude. (177)
He who, having eternally drunk the nectar of Brahman, is satisfied in the Supreme Self, considers even Indra to be insignificant; what then need be said of kings? 178.
Since supreme liberation is attained indeed through the path of the Guru, those who desire liberation should always be devoted to the Guru. 179.
"By the word of my guru, I have ascertained that I am indeed one without a second;
practicing thus constantly, one must certainly not resort to another forest. (180)
Through such practice, one attains meditative absorption (samādhi) in the very twinkling of an eye;
the sin accumulated since birth perishes at that very moment. ||181||
What is the invocation for that which is unmanifest, and what is the dismissal for that which is all-pervasive?
How can there be worship for that which is formless, and how can there be meditation upon that which is free from affliction? (182)
The Guru is Viṣṇu, consisting of sattva; as the four-faced Brahmā, he consists of rajas;
and in the form of Rudra, he consists of tamas, creating, preserving, and destroying. 183.
Having become oneself composed of Brahman, one should not look upon anything else as superior;
for there is nothing higher than the Supreme, which is all-pervading and free from affliction. 184.
Having obtained his vision, one should remain solitary, free from all attachments, desireless, and tranquil, by virtue of his grace. 185.
Whether obtained or not obtained, whether little or much, one should always enjoy it with a mind full of contentment and indeed without desire. 186.
They say that the state of omniscience belongs to the embodied soul who, pervading everything on earth, eternally blissful and eternally tranquil, rejoices wherever he may be. (187)
Wherever he dwells, O Goddess, that very place becomes a vessel of merit; thus have I described to you the characteristics of the liberated one. 188.
O Goddess, this instruction, which grants liberation through the path of the Guru, must indeed be practiced by the wise with the utmost devotion to the Guru. 189.

I bow to that Guru, the Lord, who is the foundation of all that is eternally disciplined, the creator of all Vedas and the knower of all Vedas, and the bestower of the knowledge of self and others. 190.
O beloved, even if one has studied the Vedas with their six auxiliary limbs, the Āgamas, and the treatises on the supreme self and other sciences, there is no true knowledge without a Guru. (191)
Whether one is devoted to the worship of Śiva or devoted to the worship of Viṣṇu, if one is devoid of the true nature of the Guru, all of that is indeed in vain. 192.
If worship of Śiva is performed without knowing the true nature of Śiva, that worship would be in name only, like a painted lamp, O beloved. (193)
Every action shall become fruitful through the power of initiation from a guru;
through the attainment of a guru, all things are attained, but one who is devoid of a guru is a fool. 194.
A person devoid of a guru deserves to be called an animal, an insect, or a moth, because he himself does not know his own true nature, which is the very form of Śiva. 195.
Therefore, with every effort, having abandoned all attachments and cast aside the web of scriptures, one should take refuge in the Guru alone. 196.
I worship that Guru who is the Lord himself, who, having dispelled all doubt and unified the Sudarśana, reveals the secret doctrine. 197.
A guru who is devoid of knowledge, a speaker of falsehoods, and a mere pretender should be abandoned;
for one who does not know his own state of rest, how can he bring about the peace of another? (198)
What higher knowledge can there be than that of a stone which deceives a multitude of stones?
It does not know how to cross over itself; how then could it deliver others? 199.
Alas, they are not to be honored; by the mere sight of them, delusion is produced.
One should avoid such teachers from afar and take refuge only in those who are steadfast. 200.
Heretics devoted to sin, nihilists with divisive minds, lecherous toward women, of evil conduct, ungrateful, and those who act like herons (hypocrites). ||201||

Those who have fallen from their duties, those who have lost their forbearance, those who argue with censurable logic, as well as those who are lustful, wrathful, violent, fierce, and deceitful—[these are not to be honored]. (202)
O beloved, one should not perform acts that cause the loss of knowledge, nor likewise great sins;
having reflected, one should serve a Guru who is distinct from these [sinful ones] with single-minded devotion. 203.
O Mistress of the Gods, one should not speak of this to anyone other than a disciple;
for among men, devotion alone is the cause for attaining the fruit. 204.
Secretive, firm, affectionate, silent, and well-composed—thus the guru is said to be fivefold, even when permitted to go at will on a single occasion. (205)
Everything obtained from the mouth of the Guru is fruitful and destroys sin;
whatever object is beneficial to oneself, one should not withhold that substance [from the Guru]. 206.
The object is to be offered to the Guru-deva; by that, O lady of excellent vows, I am pleased.
One should keep secret the sandals of the venerable Guru, the mudrā, and the root mantra. (207)

O Lord, I bow with my intellect, senses, vital breaths, mind, and speech at your lotus feet—that which is contemplated by those seeking liberation, who are purified through self-discipline, for the sake of the cessation of the cycle of karma. 208.
O beloved, I shall tell you what task should be performed by this [mantra];
O Goddess, it is for the benefit of the world, but one should avoid that which is merely worldly. 209.
One who is devoid of knowledge falls from the worldly dharma into the ocean of existence;
yet when knowledge is present, all action becomes non-action and is stilled. 210.
Whoever recites this with a spirit of devotion, or even hears it, or having written it down, bestows it upon others, enjoys all that fruit. ||211||
O Goddess, contemplate this *Gurugītā* constantly in your heart;
one should always recite it with joy when afflicted by the sufferings of great diseases. 212.
O beloved, each single syllable of this *Gurugītā* is a king of mantras;
other various mantras do not equal even a sixteenth part of it.
By the recitation of the *Gurugītā*, O Goddess, one obtains infinite fruit;
it removes all sins and destroys all poverty. (214)
She is the remover of untimely death and the destroyer of all calamities; she is the slayer of yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, and others, as well as thieves, tigers, and obstacles. 215.
It wards off all calamities, leprosy, and other corrupting defects;
whatever fruit is obtained from the presence of a Guru, that same fruit arises from reciting this. 216.
It shall be the remover of great diseases and the bestower of success for all forms of prosperity;
or else, in the rites of enchantment and subjugation, one should always recite it oneself. 217.
O Goddess, having sat upon a seat of kuśa grass and dūrvā, or on a white woolen blanket, one should then recite [the mantra] with a one-pointed mind, O Goddess. ||218||
White is indeed prescribed for all purposes, O Dear One, while a red seat is for subjugation;
one should always perform recitation upon a lotus-seat, which is supreme for bringing about peace and subjugation. 219.
If the seat is made of cloth, there is poverty; if of stone, the occurrence of disease;
on the bare ground, one encounters suffering; and if it is made of wood, it becomes fruitless. 220.
Success in knowledge is attained on a black antelope skin; the glory of liberation on a tiger skin; success in knowledge on a seat of kuśa grass; and indeed all success on a woolen blanket. 221.
In the southeast is ploughing; in the northwest, the destruction of enemies;
in the southwest, the vision [of the deity]; and in the northeast, knowledge itself. ||222||
Facing north during the recitation for peace, facing east likewise for subjugation;
killing is prescribed when facing south, and the acquisition of wealth when facing west. (223)
It is the supreme enchantment of all beings, the cause of bondage and liberation, and that which brings favor to the kings of the gods; it shall bring the king under one's control. ||224||
It causes the mouth to become steady, increases virtues, destroys evil deeds, and likewise grants success in virtuous actions. 225.
One shall accomplish the desired task, which removes the fear of the nine planets, destroys evil dreams, and bestows the fruits of auspicious dreams. 226.
O Śivā, this scripture of the Gītā is the supreme means for pacifying delusion and bringing about liberation from bondage; it is the abode of the knowledge of one's own true nature. 227.
Whatever desire one contemplates, that very thing one certainly attains;
it is eternally bestowing good fortune, meritorious, and the destroyer of the multitude of the three types of suffering. 228.
It constantly brings about all peace, likewise bestows excellent sons upon barren women, ensures that women do not suffer widowhood, and increases their good fortune. (229)

One who recites this without desire for personal gain—whether a widow or anyone else—shall obtain long life, health, sovereignty, and the increase of sons and grandsons; indeed, she shall attain liberation. 230.
A woman who desires it shall obtain non-widowhood in another birth;
this [rite] destroys all obstacles consisting of suffering and removes her distress. 231.
It pacifies all sins and bestows dharma, desire, wealth, and liberation;
whatever desire one contemplates, that one certainly attains. (232)

She is indeed the wish-fulfilling cow for those who desire objects of longing, the celestial wish-granting tree for all that is imagined, and the thought-gem that brings about every auspicious thing. ||233||
Whoever, having written it down, should worship it, shall attain the glory of liberation;
moreover, devotion to the guru will arise perpetually within his heart. (234)
The Śāktas, the Sauras, the Gāṇapatyas, the Vaiṣṇavas, the Śaivas, and the Pāśupatas—all of them recite this; it is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. 235.
Thus ends the second chapter of the Śrī Gurugītā, in the dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara within the Uttarakhaṇḍa of the glorious Skanda Purāṇa.
The Guru-gītā in its Extended Form:
Now begins the third chapter.
Now, O fair-faced one, I shall describe the locations for the recitation performed for specific desires:
at the edge of the ocean, on a riverbank, at a sacred ford, or in a temple of Hari or Hara. (236)
In a temple of Śakti, in a cow-pen, in an auspicious temple of all the gods, at the root of a banyan tree or a dhātrī tree, or likewise in a monastery or in Vṛndāvana. ||237||
In a pure and stainless place, or even through constant practice, one should commence this recitation with freedom from worldly attachment and in silence. (238)
Through recitation one attains victory, as well as the perfection of recitation and its fruit;
one should abandon all inferior rites and even the very place where they are performed.
They attain success in a cremation ground, at the root of a bilva tree, or likewise near the root of a vaṭa tree, at the root of a kānaka tree, or in the vicinity of a mango tree. 240.
A yellow seat is for deluding, while a black one is for malevolent rites;
it should be known that white is for the purpose of pacification, and red is proclaimed for subjugation. 241.
Performing recitation while sitting on an inferior seat yields inferior results;
likewise, reciting the Guru-gītā during travel, in battle, or amidst the perils of enemies [yields inferior results]. (242)
In Japan, one attains victory; at death, she grants liberation.
All rites are accomplished under the son of the Guru; of this there is no doubt. (243)
For one who has the guru’s mantra in his mouth, [all things] are accomplished; it is not otherwise.
Through initiation, all rites are accomplished for the son of the guru. 244.
To destroy the root of existence and to bring about the cessation of the eight bonds, the knower of reality always performs his bath in the waters of the Guru-gītā. 245.
Such a true guru is himself the manifest embodiment of the supreme knowledge of the existent and non-existent Brahman;
all his places are undoubtedly sacred. 246.
This [place] is entirely pure and sanctified by its very nature; wherever it abides, there all the hosts of gods move within that sacred field (kṣetra) and seat (pīṭha). ||247||
Whether sitting or lying down, walking or standing;
whether mounted on horses or elephants, or even while fast asleep or awake. (248)
For those who, having become pure and possessing wisdom, chant the *Gurugītā*, divine knowledge arises through the sight and touch of them. 249.
Just as water in the ocean, milk in milk, and water in water, or as space [remains distinct] when a jar is broken, so too does the self abide within the Supreme Self. 250.
In the very same way, the wise living being, possessing knowledge, always rejoices in oneness with the Supreme Self, wherever he may be, day and night. ||251||
Such a great practitioner always abides everywhere;
therefore, one should practice devotion to the guru in every possible way. ||252||
O Pārvatī, by pleasing the Guru alone one becomes liberated;
O Goddess, through his grace, the power to enjoy the siddhis such as aṇimā arises. (253)
The man of knowledge rejoices in equanimity, whether by day or by night;
such a great silent sage attains equality with the three worlds. ||254||
Then all transmigrating beings, by means of the chanting of the Guru-gītā, enjoy all their desires; this which I have spoken is the triple truth. 255.
Truth, truth, and again truth—this essence of Dharma has been declared by me.
There is no hymn equal to the Song of the Guru, nor is there any reality higher than that of the Guru. (256)
The guru is God, the guru is Dharma, and devotion to the guru is the highest austerity;
there is nothing higher than the guru—I tell you this three times. 257.
Blessed is the mother, blessed is the father, blessed is the lineage, and blessed is the one born of such a family;
and blessed, O Goddess Earth, is that land where devotion to the guru exists.

O Goddess, the performance of sacrifices, vows, and austerities throughout tens of millions of births until the end of the aeon—all these become fruitful merely through the satisfaction of the Guru. (259)
The body, the senses, the vital breath, wealth, one's own kin and relatives, the mother’s family, the father’s family, and the teacher—of this there is no doubt. (260)
For those unfortunate and powerless people who do not give their consent, being averse to service toward their gurus, are cooked in a foul hell. 261.
Knowledge, wealth, and strength—these are of no avail for those who lack the grace of their guru; they go downward, O Pārvatī. (262)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; the gods, the ancestors, and the kinnaras; the siddhas, cāraṇas, and yakṣas; and other sages and people. ||263||
Devotion to the Guru is the supreme sacred ford; any other purpose is meaningless.
O Goddess, the lotus feet of the illustrious Guru embody all sacred fords. 264.
Delighting in the enjoyment of young maidens, these dull-witted men turn their backs on their own beloved wives;
beyond this, O Goddess, my dear, I have said nothing further. 265.
O fair-faced one, this secret, though unclear, must be spoken; it is to be well-guarded before you for the sake of my own pleasure. 266.
O Pārvatī, O Mahāmāyā, you must not speak thus; please touch my feet, including those of the Lord, Gaṇeśa, and others such as the Vaiṣṇavas. 267.
The *Gurugītā* should never be spoken even mentally to one who is non-devoted, deceitful, fraudulent, a heretic, an atheist, or the like. (268)
There are many gurus who seize the wealth of their disciples;
I consider that one alone to be rare who steals away the very heart of the disciple. (269)
One who possesses skill, discernment, knowledge of the supreme self, and purity—his status as a teacher shines forth, for his mind is stainless. (270)
The gurus are stainless, peaceful, virtuous, and moderate in speech; they are entirely free from desire and anger, possessed of noble conduct, and have conquered their senses. ||271||
Gurus are recorded as being of many kinds, distinguished by their roles as indicators and so forth;
therefore, having personally and thoroughly examined them, the wise person should serve one who is established in reality. 272.
Likewise, O Goddess, that worldly external scripture which is a mere web of syllables—when it has been thoroughly mastered therein, he is known as a true teacher. (273)

O Pārvatī, know that the teacher who imparts the knowledge appropriate for one's caste and stage of life, which establishes the rules of dharma and adharma, is the true Guru; the reciter, however, is merely a reader.
O Pārvatī, he who is the instructor of the five-syllabled mantra and others shall be the enlightening Guru; this one is the most excellent of both. (275)
The wise who perceive reality call one who teaches trivial mantras for the sake of delusion, killing, subjugation, and so forth, a forbidden guru. (276)
O beloved, he who, having pointed out that saṃsāra is an abode of peril, shows the path of detachment, is designated as a guru. 277.
O Pārvatī, the teacher of such statements as "That thou art" is declared to be the Guru named Kāraṇa, the remover of the disease of worldly existence. ||278||
He who is skilled in uprooting the entire mass of all doubts and who destroys the fear of birth and death is considered the supreme guru. 279.
This great Guru is obtained through merit accumulated over many lifetimes;
having found him, the disciple never again enters the bondage of saṃsāra. 280.
Thus, O Pārvatī, there are many kinds of gurus in the world;
among them, however, the supreme guru alone is to be served with every effort. (281)
But one who has been forbidden from being a teacher or a disciple, and is corrupted by evil intentions, does not return to mortal existence until the dissolution of Brahmā. ||282||
Having heard these words of Mahādeva in such a manner, the Great Goddess,
her mind utterly overwhelmed, questioned Śaṅkara.
Pārvatī said:
"Salutations to you, O God of gods; there is something I wish to hear here.
Having now heard your words, my mind has become exceedingly agitated. (284)
If those who are themselves deluded, terrified of death, and have desisted from virtuous deeds, should by fate encounter a guru who prohibits them [from evil], what indeed will be their destiny? 285.
The illustrious Mahādeva said:
Listen to this truth, O Goddess: when a man becomes dispassionate, then he is declared by the crest-jewels of the Vedas to be qualified [for this path]. (286)
He by whom Brahman—indivisible, of a single essence, eternally free, and free from affliction—is revealed within oneself, he alone shall be the Guru for this [seeker]. ||287||
Just as the ocean is the king of all waters, O Pārvatī, so this supreme preceptor is the king among all gurus. 288.

Free from delusion and the like, peaceful, eternally satisfied, and without dependence, he who has rendered the majesty of Brahmā and Viṣṇu as insignificant as a blade of grass is the supreme Guru. ||289||
Independent in all times and places, unmoving and happy, the supreme Guru is indeed satisfied by the tasting of the undivided single essence. 290.
Free from both duality and non-duality, possessing the light of self-realization, the destroyer of the blinding darkness of ignorance, he is the omniscient supreme teacher. ||291||
He by whose mere sight the mind becomes serene, and in whom fortitude and peace arise spontaneously—he shall be the supreme teacher. (292)
Having observed the net of accomplishments belonging to yogins and mantra-practitioners, he whose mental activity regards them as insignificant is the supreme teacher. (293)
He who, beholding his own body as a corpse and likewise his own self as non-dual, destroys the delusion regarding women and gold—he shall be the supreme teacher. (294)
O Pārvatī, listen: the knower of reality is of two kinds—the silent and the eloquent.
O beloved, in this world, no gain whatsoever is obtained through silence.
He is eloquent and capable of crossing over the turbulent ocean of saṃsāra, for he is the dispeller of doubt through scripture, reasoning, and direct experience. (296)
O Goddess, by the recitation of the Guru’s name, even the sins accumulated over many lifetimes go to destruction; there is not even the slightest doubt about this. 297.
There is no deity equal to the venerable Guru; there is no father equal to the venerable Guru.
There is no practice on this earth equal to the meditation upon the Guru—there is none, there is none. (298)
Lineage, wealth, strength, sacred learning, and these kinsmen and brothers—none of these are of use at the time of death; for the Guru alone is the savior. 299.
The family itself becomes pure through truth and service to one's own guru;
all the gods, beginning with Brahmā, become satisfied by the propitiation of the guru. (300)
For the Guru alone knows the nature of the immutable God;
that knowledge comes through His grace, and not otherwise, even by means of millions of scriptures. (301)

O Goddess, even that which is performed by one devoid of knowledge of the true nature [of reality] becomes as if unperformed; all such acts as austerity and recitation are like the prattle of a child. (302)
Some [worship] Śiva, some Hari, some Brahmā, and others the Goddess Śakti; knowing them thus, men dispute in vain. (303)
Those who have turned their backs on the initiation of a guru do not know the supreme reality;
deluded and devoid of self-knowledge, they are indeed equal to bound souls (paśu). ||304||
Therefore, O beloved, for the sake of attaining liberation, one should worship the Guru alone;
without the Guru, the deluded do not know that supreme state. (305)
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder, and all karmas are exhausted through the compassion of the Guru, O Śivā. 306.
One who has performed devotion to the guru in accordance with the Vedas and Shastras, and especially one devoted to the guru, is liberated from even the most terrible sin. ||307||
Having abandoned harmful associations, one should abandon evil deeds;
for him whose mind bears this sign, initiation is ordained. (308)
And for one who is intent on the renunciation of the mind, who is free from anger and pride, and who has abandoned the state of duality, initiation is prescribed. ||309||
Initiation is prescribed for one who possesses these characteristics, who delights in the welfare of all beings, and whose life is stainless. (310)
Previously, the entire network of initiations was described as being accompanied by ritual action;
that which was proclaimed by Śiva includes the initiations of mantra along with all their primary and secondary limbs. 311.
Who indeed, without the initiation of a guru—which bestows union with the guru and is devoid of [worldly] ritual action—could be a protector of the conduct of a guru? 312.
Whether he is capable or incapable, by taking refuge at the feet of the Teacher, his birth becomes fruitful, bestowing the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||313||
O Goddess, this should always be spoken for my own pleasure to one whose mind is fully ripened and who is endowed with faith and devotion. 314.
O Śivā, this secret of all scriptures, which bestows the Gītā-śāstra, should be spoken only after thorough examination to a practitioner whose soul is devoted to me. 315.
And for the wise practitioner whose mind has been purified through the ripening of virtuous deeds, the *Gurugītā* should indeed be taught with great care. 316.
This [teaching] should never be spoken to an atheist, an ungrateful person, a hypocrite, a rogue, one who lacks devotion, or one who is divisive. ||317||
The *Gurugītā* should not, by its very nature, be spoken to one who is lustful toward women, to a fool, to one whose mind is afflicted by passion, or to a slanderer. (318)
O Goddess Śivā, this scripture of the Gītā pacifies all sins, wards off all calamities, and removes both birth and death. 319.
O Goddess, O Śivā, this essence of the Vedas has been told to you in its entirety and in brief;
there is no other way for men to attain the true goal without the station of the Guru. 320.
This goal does not appeal to one who has committed sins over many lifetimes;
therefore, for the sake of ceasing the bondage of birth, one should always devote oneself to the Guru alone. ||321||
"I alone am the entire universe; I alone am the supreme state.
I bow down to that Guru from whom such knowledge may arise. (322)
Enough with conceptual constructions; I alone am absolute, and this entire universe, both moving and unmoving, resides within me.
He who has revealed this secret to me is indeed my sole Guru, worthy of worship. 323.
He has neither end, nor beginning, nor middle; indeed, he has no hands or feet, no name or lineage, no scripture;
he has no birth, no caste, and is not a man, nor a neuter, nor a woman. (324)

I bow to that true Guru, who is neither form nor transformation, for whom there is neither birth nor death, neither merit nor sin, and who is neither non-reality nor reality—He alone is the innate, perfectly harmonious One. 325.

Salutations eternally to Him who is the eternal, the truth, the nature of consciousness, the ever-new, the auspicious, the highest of the high, the pure, the enlightened, the stainless, and the crest-jewel of all gurus. 326.
Salutation to the Supreme Self, who is all-pervasive and whose nature is truth, consciousness, and bliss;
salutation to the venerable Guru, the embodiment of light and joy. 327.
Salutations to the Guru, who is the embodiment of truth and bliss, who bestows the singular happiness of awakening, who is known through the Vedanta, and who is the witness of the intellect. 328.
Salutations to you, O Lord, Blessed One, the auspicious one in the form of the Guru, who has assumed manifold forms for the sake of perfecting the descent of knowledge. 329

Salutations to You, the mass of consciousness, who are ever-new and of ever-new form, whose single nature is the ultimate reality, and who are the sun that shatters the darkness of all ignorance. 330.

To the independent one who has assumed a form out of compassion, whose nature is auspiciousness; to the one who is dependent upon his devotees, appearing in an auspicious form for those who are worthy of liberation. ||331||

For the sake of discernment for the discerning, for the sake of investigation for the investigators, for the sake of illumination for the illuminators—to the one who is the very form of knowledge for the wise. ||332||
In front, on the sides, behind, above, and below, always perform my worship in the form of being ever-minded toward me; thus prepare a seat for me.
I bow to the glorious Guru, supreme bliss, whose very form is bliss;
by his mere presence, my mind is directed toward the bliss of consciousness. 334.
Salutations be to you, O Guru, whose form is innate bliss;
the nectar of whose speech destroys the poison known as saṃsāra. (335)

By means of various reasoned instructions, the lineage of disciples was delivered; through the realization of the essence produced thereby, they attained the unshakable state of the Guru’s heart. 336.
Salutations to you, the infallible one, whose mind is fixed on the Guru, the Supreme Self, who is independent of all systems of thought, and whose form is the mass of consciousness and bliss. ||337||
Salutations to the infallible Guru, whose nature is both knowledge and ignorance, who is the guide for disciples upon the true path, and an ocean of the nectar of compassion. 338.

Obeisance to you, whose nature is the bliss of consciousness—the teacher who has not fallen from his state, the bridge for disciples across the ocean of saṃsāra, and the singular lion among those who act solely out of devotion. 339.
There is no deity equal to the name of the Guru, nor are there fathers or kinsmen;
there is no master equal to the name of the Guru, nor is there such a supreme state. ||340||
He who does not respect the guru who has bestowed upon him even a single syllable will, after passing through a hundred births as a dog, be born among the Cāṇḍālas. ||341||
From abandoning the guru comes death; from abandoning the mantra comes poverty.
One who abandons both the guru and the mantra shall go to the Raurava hell. (342)
The Guru is the protector from the wrath of Śiva, but Śiva is not the protector from the wrath of the Guru;
therefore, with every effort, one must not transgress the command of the Guru. 343.

I pay homage to the mantra of the King of Gurus, which is the sole spell for being rescued from the ocean of saṃsāra, the perfected mantra worshipped by Brahmā and the other gods and sages, the mantra that destroys poverty, suffering, and the disease of existence, and the remover of great fears. (344)
Seven crores of great mantras may cause the mind to go astray;
yet the single great mantra is the two syllables "Gu-ru. (345)
Having spoken thus to Pārvatī, Mahādeva spoke again:
"O Goddess, listen to this supreme truth which brings happiness. (346)
O Goddess, this entire reality of the Guru has been declared in brief;
this secret, which is unmanifest, one should not speak of to just anyone. 347.
O Goddess, these words of mine shall not be false; they are of the nature of truth.
There is no hymn equal to the *Gurugītā* upon the surface of the earth—there is none, there is none. (348)
O Goddess, one should never recite this *Gurugītā*, which destroys the suffering of worldly existence, in the presence of one who is devoid of initiation from a guru. 349.
This is a secret, O Maheśvarī, an absolute secret; this cannot be obtained by a sinner.
Through the ripening of merit accumulated over many births, a human being obtains this reality from the Guru. ||350||
By whose grace I am indeed everything, and everything is imagined within me alone;
thus knowing the true nature of the eternal Self, I bow perpetually at his lotus feet. 351.
O Lord, grant me your grace by bestowing the light of knowledge upon me, who am blinded by the darkness of ignorance and whose mind is assailed by sense objects. 352.
Thus ends the third chapter of the Śrī Gurugītā.
Thus ends the *Gurugītā* within the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the *Śrī Skandapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī.
May this be an offering to the venerable Guru Dattātreya.
The Short Version of the Gurugītā.
Śrī.
The Five Verses on the Holy Guru’s Sandals (Śrī Gurupādukā Pañcakam)

Oṃ, salutations to the gurus; salutations to the sandals of the gurus. Salutations to the supreme ones; salutations to the sandals of the supreme ones. Salutations again and again to the sandals of the Siddheśvara Ācārya; salutations to the sandals of the venerable guru.
By means of the syllable Aiṃ, the syllable Hrīṃ, and the syllable Śrīṃ, which are joined with the secret [mantra] and possess great majesty through their hidden meaning. ||1||
Salutations again and again to the two venerable Guru’s sandals, which expound the essential points of the syllable Oṃ. ||2||

Salutations again and again to the two venerable sandals of the Guru, which spread the realization of that Brahman which manifests in all forms, such as the Hotṛ-fire, the Hautrāgni, the oblation, the Hotṛ-priest, the Homa, and so forth. ||3||

Salutations again and again to the lotus-feet of the venerable Guru, which are like a pair of Garuḍas for the swarm of serpents such as desire, which bestow the treasure of discernment and dispassion, which grant awakening, and which swiftly bestow liberation. ||4||

Salutations again and again to the venerable sandals of the Guru, which act as a boat for crossing the infinite ocean of saṃsāra, which bestow steadfast devotion, and which serve as the submarine fire that dries up the ocean of dullness. ||5||
Oṃ, peace, peace, peace.
Now begins the Śrī Gurugītā.
Obeisance to Śrī Gaṇeśa. Obeisance to Śrī Sarasvatī. Obeisance to the Śrī Gurus. Om.
Of this mantra of the Śrīgurugītā-stotra, the Blessed Sadāśiva is the seer (ṛṣi); various meters (chandas) are the meter; the Supreme Self of the Śrīguru is the deity (devatā);
"haṃ" is the seed-syllable (bīja); "saḥ" is the power (śakti); and "kroṃ" is the pin (kīlaka).
The application is for the purpose of attaining the grace of the Śrī Guru during the recitation.
Now, the meditation:

By the two swans, who are the causes of the universe, whose lotus-petals are turned back, who are divine, who are carved upon all things, and who dwell in many bodies, [the world was created] freely according to their own will.

One should meditate upon the all-pervading, eternal Guru, who is the manifestation of that [light], the state of Śambhu, the foot that grasps the sprout of the lamp, and whose form consists of perceptible syllables.
The application (viniyoga) is for the purpose of accomplishing the fourfold aims of human life through the recitation of this mantra.
Now begins the *Śrīgurugītā*.
Sūta said:
On the beautiful peak of Kailāsa, Pārvatī, having bowed with devotion to Śaṅkara, the leader who bestows devotion, questioned him. ||1||
The Goddess said:
Oṃ, salutations, O God, Lord of gods, Supreme beyond the supreme, Teacher of the world!
O Sadāśiva, Mahādeva, grant me the initiation of the Guru. ||2||
"O Lord, by what path may one become composed of Brahman?
Have mercy on me, O Master; I bow at your feet. (3)
The Lord said: "O Goddess, you are my very form; for the sake of your pleasure, I shall speak.
No one has ever before asked a question so beneficial to the world. (4)
Listen, O fair-faced one, as I declare that which is difficult to find in the three worlds: there is no truth other than Brahman apart from the Guru; this is the truth, the absolute truth. (5)

The Vedas, Śāstras, Purāṇas, and histories such as the Itihāsas; the sciences of mantras, yantras, and the like; the Smṛtis, and rites for eradication (uccāṭana) and so forth—[all these he knows]. (6)
The Śaiva, Śākta, Āgama, and other various scriptures here cause the corruption of living beings whose minds are deluded. (7)
Fools perform sacrifice, vows, austerity, charity, recitation, pilgrimage, and likewise the service of the guru, all without understanding the true nature of the guru. 8.
There is nothing more real than the Self perceived as the Guru; this is the truth, the truth, without a doubt.
Therefore, wise men must indeed exert effort for the sake of attaining that. 9.
The secret science is the world-illusion (jaganmāyā), which arises from ignorance within the body;
its emergence is described by the term "Guru" through the light of that [knowledge]. 10.
Since an embodied soul becomes Brahman through purification from all sins by serving the feet of the venerable Guru, I shall speak to you for the sake of your grace. 11.
Having recollected the lotus feet of the Guru, a person should hold water upon his head;
he thereby obtains the fruit of bathing in all sacred fords (tīrthas). ||12||
The water from the feet of the Guru thoroughly dries up the mire of sin, kindles the splendors of knowledge, and enables one to cross the ocean of saṃsāra. 13.
One should drink the water from the feet of the Guru for the sake of attaining knowledge and dispassion—that which uproots the foundation of ignorance and wards off the cycle of birth and action. 14.
Having drunk the water from the feet of the guru, one should eat the remnants of the guru's food;
one should always meditate upon the form of the guru and always recite the mantra of the guru. 15.
The sacred field of Kāśī is his dwelling; the water from the feet of the Jāhnavī is his [sustenance];
Viśveśvara himself is his manifest guru; and the Tāraka Brahman is his certain goal. ||16||
The water from the feet of the Guru is that very Gayā, and he is the imperishable banyan tree;
he is Prayāga, the king of holy places. Salutations again and again to the embodiment of the Guru. 17.
One should constantly meditate on the form of the Guru and always recite the name of the Guru; one should carry out the command of the Guru and not conceive of anything other than the Guru. 18.
The Brahman residing in the mouth of the Guru is attained through his grace;
one should always perform meditation upon the Guru, just as a woman of noble family meditates upon her husband. 19.
Having renounced one's own hermitage, one's own caste, and everything that increases the nourishment of one's own fame—one should think of nothing other than the Guru. 20.
Thinking of Me alone, the supreme state is easily attained;
therefore, with every effort, perform the propitiation of the Guru. 21.
In the three worlds, the gods, asuras, and pannagas are clearly proclaimers [of this truth]:
the Vidyā residing in the mouth of the Guru is obtained only through devotion to the Guru. 22.
The syllable *gu* is darkness, and the syllable *ru* is said to be light;
Brahman is the devourer of ignorance—it is the Guru alone, without a doubt. (23)
The first syllable is *gu*, which illuminates the qualities such as Māyā;
the second syllable is *ru*, which destroys the delusion of Brahmā’s Māyā. ||24||
Thus, this supreme station of the Guru, difficult even for the gods to attain, is worshipped by the hosts of Hāhā and Hūhū, as well as by the Gandharvas. (25)
It is certain that for all of them there is no reality higher than the Guru;
[he is their] seat, bed, clothing, ornament, vehicle, and so forth. (26)
The practitioner must offer that which causes satisfaction to the guru;
he should perform the propitiation of the guru and offer his very life. 27.
One should always propitiate the guru through action, mind, and speech;
having bowed with a long staff, one should remain free from shame in the presence of the guru. 28.
One should offer one's body, senses, and vital breaths to the true gurus;
one should offer everything, including oneself, one's wife, and so forth, to the true gurus. (29)
O fair-faced one, one should not be deceived by worms, insects, ashes, excrement, foul odors, feces and urine, phlegm, blood, skin, or flesh. (30)
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom all those who have climbed the tree of saṃsāra and are falling into the ocean of hell have been uplifted. 31.
The Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru alone is the Supreme Brahman—salutations to that illustrious Guru. 32.
Salutations to the Guru, who is the cause of the worlds themselves, the bridge across the ocean of saṃsāra, the source of all sciences, and the embodiment of auspiciousness. 33.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whom the eye of one blinded by the darkness of ignorance was opened with the applicator of the collyrium of knowledge. 34.
You are my father, you are my mother, you are my kinsman, and you are my deity;
salutations to that venerable Guru for the sake of awakening me from the cycle of worldly existence. ||35||
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whose truth the world becomes real, by whose light it shines, and by whose bliss all beings rejoice. 36.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by whose abiding presence this world appears as true in the form of the sun, and through whose love even a son becomes dear. 37.
Salutation to that venerable Guru, by whom this mind is made to will, yet he does not will; [he who is present] in waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and so forth. 38.
Salutation to that venerable Guru, whose knowledge renders this entire universe invisible as a distinct multiplicity, and who is the embodiment of the single form of pure existence. 39.
He whose [intellect] does not conceive is the one who has realized; he who conceives does not know.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, whose nature is non-dual. 40.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, who is the causal form in which the effect appears as the form of the effect, yet remains the causal form itself. 41.
All this is of manifold forms, yet no differentiation exists in it;
to Him who is both effect and cause, to that venerable Guru, obeisance! 42.
I bow to the venerable Guru, whose pair of lotus feet wards off the heat of dualities and always delivers one from all calamities. 43.
When Śiva is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, Śiva is not.
Therefore, with every effort, one should go for refuge to the venerable Guru. 44.
I bow to the pair of the Guru’s feet, which are the object of speech, mind, and heart;
they are distinguished by white and red radiance, and are the supreme essence of Śiva and Śakti. 45.

He who bestows the syllable *gu*, which transcends the qualities (*guṇa*), and the syllable *ru*, which is devoid of form, and whose own nature transcends the qualities—he is known as the Guru. ||46||
O beloved, the venerable Guru has been described as having three eyes, being the witness of all, possessing no four arms, being infallible, and having no four faces—just like Brahmā. 47.
I join my palms in reverence to increase the ocean of compassion, by whose grace a living being attains liberation from the manifold cycle of existence. 48.
The supreme form of the illustrious Guru is the nectar for those with the eye of discernment;
those of dull fortune do not behold it, just as the blind do not see the rising of the sun. 49.
O beloved, one should daily offer salutations with devotion to that direction in which the pair of feet of Śrīnātha shines. 50.
O Noble Lady, this salutation with palms joined is constantly offered toward that direction,
which is made resonant by bees and the wise—
the direction where the Blessed One, the sovereign of teachers, remains ever awake.
The eternal witness of the drama of the creation and dissolution of the universe. ||51||
I bow to the triad of Gurus beginning with Śrīnātha, Gaṇapati, the three Pīṭhas, Bhairava,
the Siddhaugha, the triad of Baṭukas, the pair of feet, the triad of Dūtīs, the Śāmbhava [tradition],
the eight Vīreśas, the four groups of sixty-nine, and the fivefold Vīrāvalī.
I salute the circle of gurus together with the glorious Mālinī, the king of mantras. 52.

When that [state] has arisen, the powerful wind itself perishes at that very moment— [the wind] which had been practiced through all the long breaths, which causes disease, which is difficult to perform, which involves many methods, which is painful in nature, and which is hard to conquer.
To attain that innate nature, you should incessantly serve a single Guru. ||53||
Meditation upon one's own teacher is indeed meditation upon the infinite Śiva;
and the chanting of one's own teacher’s name is likewise [the chanting of his].
This would be the glorification of the infinite Śiva. ||54||
We worship that Lord and Guide, even a single atom of whose foot-dust acts as a causeway across the ocean of saṃsāra. 55.
Salutations to that illustrious Lord of Teachers, by receiving whose grace one may cast off great ignorance; may he grant the fulfillment of our desires. (56)
The lotus-foot, which destroys the forest fire of all saṃsāra, is situated within the lunar orb in the center of the white lotus at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). ||57||

One should meditate upon the Guru situated in the center of the thousand-petaled mandala lotus with three lines, which begins with the letter 'a', as well as in the triangle on the side of the *haṃsa*. 58.

May you be one who has fashioned the creation of all worlds, who has conceived the nourishment of all things, whose vision is the entirety of the Vedas, whose view renders worldly prosperity meaningless, who wipes away all defects, whose sole focus is the meaning of that supreme state (Brahman), who is the highest among those possessed of virtues, and whose vision is fixed solely on the path to liberation. 59.
The supporting pillar for establishing the stage of the entire universe, a rain of the aesthetic flavor of compassion, the unified totality of the garland of principles,
the creator of all conventions, and the vision of Being-Consciousness-Bliss.
May the divine vision of the venerable Guru abide within me eternally. ||60||
I consider this king of mantras, which is pure like fire and surrounded on all sides by a circle of flames, to protect me from death day and night through its meditative power. 61.
It moves, and it moves not; it is far, and it is near;
it is within all this, and it is outside of all this. 62.
I am unborn, I am ageless, and I am myself without beginning or end;
I am changeless, consciousness and bliss, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.
It is unprecedented, supreme, eternal, self-luminous, and free from affliction;
it is the stainless, supreme space, fixed, blissful, and immutable.
One should always remember the fourfold means—scripture, direct perception, tradition, and inference—as well as one's own self, austerity, sacred knowledge, and the teacher. 65.
O Mahāmati, I shall tell you that which is to be done after reflection;
having observed your goodness, it now abides within you. (66)
Salutations to that venerable Guru by whom that state was revealed—the state which is of the nature of an unbroken circle and by which all that is moving and unmoving is pervaded. ||67||
Salutations to that venerable Guru, whose lotus feet are adorned by the crest-jewels of all the Vedas, and who is the sun to the lotus of the Vedānta. 68.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, by the mere remembrance of whom knowledge arises spontaneously, and who is the attainment of all things. 69.
Salutation to that venerable Guru, who is consciousness, eternal, peaceful, beyond the ether, stainless, and transcendent of sound, the point, and the creative energies.
Salutation to that venerable Guru by whom the entire world—whether stationary or moving, and likewise all that is mobile and immobile—is pervaded. 71.
Salutations to that venerable Guru, who is mounted upon the power of knowledge, adorned with the garland of the principles (tattvas), and the bestower of both worldly enjoyment and liberation. ||72||
Salutations to that venerable Guru, who has attained [the state] through many births and who burns away all karma by the power of the knowledge of his own Self. 73.
There is no reality greater than the Guru; there is no austerity greater than the Guru.
There is no truth higher than knowledge. Salutations to that illustrious Guru. (74)
The Lord of Men, Śrī Jagannātha, my guru, the teacher of the three worlds, who is my own self and the self of all beings—to that glorious guru, obeisance! (75)
The root of meditation is the form of the Guru; the root of worship is the feet of the Guru;
the root of mantra is the word of the Guru. Salutations to that illustrious Guru. ||76||
The Guru is the beginning and is without beginning; the Guru is the supreme deity.
There is nothing higher than the Guru; salutations to that illustrious Guru. ||77||
The fruit of bathing in all the holy fords extending to the seven oceans is not difficult to attain even when compared to a thousandth part of a drop of water from the feet of the Guru. (78)
When Hari is angry, the Guru is the protector; when the Guru is angry, there is no one at all.
Therefore, with every effort, one should go for refuge to the venerable Guru. 79.
The Guru alone is the entire universe, consisting of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
