there is nothing higher than the Guru, therefore one should worship the Guru. 80.
Knowledge, accompanied by discernment, is obtained through devotion to the guru;
there is nothing higher than the guru, and he is the object of meditation for those who follow the path of the guru. (81)
Since there is nothing higher than this, as the Śruti declares "not this, not this" (neti neti), one should constantly worship the guru with both mind and speech. 82.

By the grace and favor of the Guru, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Sadāśiva are capable of creation and the other cosmic functions; indeed, it is solely through service to the Guru that they possess this power. 83.
The gods, kinnaras, gandharvas, ancestors, yakṣas, cāraṇas, and even the sages do not know the method for serving one's preceptor. ||84||
Possessed of the power of austerity and knowledge through the pride of great egoism, they revolve in the whirlpool of the cave of saṃsāra like jars on a water-wheel. ||85||
Neither gods, nor Gandharvas, nor ancestors, nor Yakṣas, nor Kinnaras, nor sages, nor all the Siddhas are liberated for one who is averse to service toward his guru. (86)
Listen, O Great Goddess, to the description of meditation, which bestows all bliss, eternally produces all happiness, and grants both worldly enjoyment and liberation. 87.
I remember the glorious Supreme Brahman, the Guru; I speak of the glorious Supreme Brahman, the Guru;
I bow to the glorious Supreme Brahman, the Guru; I worship the glorious Supreme Brahman, the Guru. ||88||
The bliss of Brahman, which bestows supreme happiness, is pure consciousness personified;
it transcends all dualities, is like the sky, and is the objective reality indicated by such mahāvākyas as "That thou art.
It is one, eternal, stainless, immovable, and the witness of all cognitions.
I bow to that true Guru who has transcended all states of being and is devoid of the three qualities (guṇas).
I bow to the Guru who is Brahman—eternal, pure, beyond appearance, formless, untainted, eternally awakened, and the bliss of consciousness. ||89-90||

One should meditate upon the Guru, whose divine form is seated upon a lion-throne situated in the center of the pericarp of the heart-lotus; he shines with the luster of a digit of the moon and holds a book of consciousness, a rosary, and the gesture of granting desired boons. 91.
Clad in white garments, adorned with white unguents and flowers, decorated with pearls, joyful, and two-eyed;
with his divine Śakti seated upon the lap of his left side, possessing a gentle smile, he is a dense treasury of compassion. ||92||

I perpetually bow to the glorious Guru—the blissful one who creates bliss, the serene one whose nature is knowledge, endowed with innate awakening, the lord of yogis worthy of praise, and the physician for the disease of worldly existence. 93.
I bow to Him in whom the fivefold activity—consisting of creation, maintenance, destruction, restraint, and grace—shines eternally. (94)

In the morning, one should first recite the name and then meditate upon the Guru, who has two eyes and two arms, who bestows boons and fearlessness, and who is peaceful, seated upon a white lotus on the crown of the head. 95.
Nothing is superior to the Guru, nothing is superior to the Guru, nothing is superior to the Guru, nothing is superior to the Guru;
by the teaching of Śiva, by the teaching of Śiva, by the teaching of Śiva, by the teaching of Śiva. ||96||
This alone is auspicious, this alone is auspicious, this alone is auspicious, this alone is auspicious;
through my teaching, through my teaching, through my teaching, through my teaching. (97)
Having meditated upon the Guru in this manner, knowledge arises spontaneously;
one should then contemplate, "By the grace of that true Guru, I am liberated. (98)
One should effect purification of the mind by the path shown by the Guru;
one should break down everything that falls within the scope of the self as impermanent. 99.
The object of knowledge is the nature of all things, and the mind is called the means of knowledge;
one should make the knowledge equal to the object of knowledge—there is no other second path. 100.
Having heard this, O Great Goddess, whoever reviles the Guru goes to a terrible hell for as long as the moon and sun endure. 101.
One should remember the Guru for as long as the end of the kalpa lasts; one must not neglect the Guru, even if one becomes independent. 102.
Wise disciples should never utter the sound "huṃ," nor should they ever speak untruth in the presence of their guru. (103)
Having treated his teacher with contempt, having uttered "huṃ" against him, or having defeated him in debate, he shall become a *brahmarākṣasa* in a waterless forest region. (104)
O Pārvatī, whether one has been cursed by sages, serpents, or even gods, or even out of fear of death at the appointed time, he protects his gurus.
For even the gods and others are powerless, and likewise the sages;
by the curse of their preceptor, they quickly go to destruction—of this there is no doubt. (106)
O Goddess, this king of mantras consists of two syllables: "gu-ru.
According to the statement of the meaning of the Vedas and the Smṛtis, the Guru is the manifest supreme state. (107)

Those who, without understanding the Śruti and Smṛti, are merely servants to their gurus, they alone are declared to be true renunciants (saṃnyāsins); others are merely wearers of the outward garb. ||108||
One should realize the eternal Brahman as formless, devoid of qualities, and supreme;
all is Brahman, free from appearances, just as one lamp illuminates another lamp. (109)
By the grace and favor of the Guru, one should behold the Self-delighting [Ātman];
through this path of the Guru, knowledge of one's own Self arises. 110.
I bow to that which consists of the universe—the moving and the unmoving—from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—which has the nature of the Supreme Self. 111.
I bow to the Guru, who is existence-consciousness-bliss, eternally beyond duality, perpetual, complete, formless, devoid of attributes, and established in his own Self. 112.
That which is to be meditated upon is higher than the highest, eternally producing bliss, situated in the center of the space of the heart, and resembling pure crystal. (113)
Just as the form of a crystal statue is seen in a mirror, so too is the form of consciousness, which is bliss, perceived within the Self as "I am He. (114)
Listen as I describe that state which flashes forth for one meditating upon the Person the size of a thumb, consisting of consciousness, within the heart. 115.
I am unborn, I am immortal, indeed I am without beginning or end;
I am changeless, consciousness-bliss, subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.
It is without prior or posterior, eternal, self-luminous, and free from affliction;
it is the stainless supreme ether, fixed, blissful, and imperishable.
O Pārvatī, one should know that Brahman is the non-domain, yet it is to be reached; it is devoid of name and form, and is soundless—such is its own nature.
Just as fragrance exists by its own nature in camphor, flowers, and the like, so too does the eternal Brahman exist by its own nature through qualities such as coldness and heat. 117.
Having oneself become such a knower, one should remain wherever one may be;
there, meditation becomes like that of a worm or a bee. 118.
Having thus performed meditation on the Guru, one becomes identical with Brahman oneself;
liberated in the piṇḍa, the pada, and the rūpa, there is no doubt in this matter. ||119||
Having oneself become identical with all, one should behold the supreme reality;
there is nothing else higher than the highest, for all this is without a foundation.
Having obtained its vision, which is free from all attachment, one should remain alone, desireless, and peaceful by virtue of its grace. 121.
Whether it has been obtained or not obtained, whether it be small or great, one should always enjoy it with a mind of constant contentment and indeed without desire. 122.
The wise say that the state of omniscience belongs to the embodied soul who consists of all things;
eternally blissful and eternally tranquil, he rejoices wherever he may be. (123)
Wherever he remains, O Goddess, that place becomes a vessel of merit; thus have I described the characteristics of the liberated one before you. 124.
Likewise, O Goddess, instruction through the path of the Guru bestows liberation;
devotion to the Guru and meditation—all this has been proclaimed to you. (125)
O Mahāmati, I shall tell you what task should be performed by this [mantra], which is beneficial to the world; O Goddess, one should not practice that which is merely worldly. 126.
Those devoid of knowledge go from worldly action into the ocean of existence;
but the man of knowledge should contemplate all action performed as being without action. 127.
But if one reads or hears this with a spirit of devotion, having written it down, that gift should be bestowed along with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). ||128||
O Goddess, I have proclaimed this pure reality consisting of the Guru-gītā;
for the sake of destroying the disease of worldly existence, one should always recite it oneself. 129.
One should mutter this king of mantras, consisting of even a single syllable of the Gurugītā;
other various mantras are not worth even a sixteenth part of it. 130.
By the recitation of the Guru-gītā, one indeed attains infinite fruit;
it pacifies all sins and destroys all poverty. (131)
It removes the fear of untimely death, destroys all calamities, and dispels the fear of yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, thieves, and tigers. (132)
It shall remove all great diseases and bestow all prosperity and supernatural powers; or else, one should always personally recite it for the purpose of enchantment or subjugation. 133.
O Goddess, having sat upon a seat made of kuśa grass, or dūrvā grass, or a white woolen blanket, one should then recite [the mantra] with a one-pointed mind, O Goddess. 134.
The object of meditation should be white for the sake of peace; O Dear One, a red seat is used for subjugation;
it is black in color for malevolent rites, and yellow in color for the acquisition of wealth. 135.
One desiring peace should face north; for subjugation, one should recite facing east; killing is said to be performed facing south, and the acquisition of wealth facing west. (136)
In the southeast lies cultivation; in the northwest, the destruction of enemies;
in the southwest, vision; and in the northeast, knowledge itself.
If the seat is made of cloth, there is poverty; if it is stone, the occurrence of disease;
on earth, one encounters suffering; and if it is wood, it becomes fruitless.
Success in knowledge is attained on a black antelope skin, and the glory of liberation on a tiger skin;
success in knowledge is attained on a seat of kuśa grass, while all successes are attained on a woolen blanket.
It shall be enchanting to all beings and a means for liberation from bondage;
it shall bring favor to the king of the gods and bring all the worlds under one's control. ||137||
It causes the stabilization of all things, increases virtues, destroys evil deeds, and brings about the accomplishment of virtuous actions. (138)
It shall accomplish unaccomplished tasks, remove the fear of the nine planets, destroy evil dreams, and bestow the fruits of auspicious dreams. 139.
It constantly brings about all peace, likewise bestows noble sons upon the barren, ensures that women do not suffer widowhood, and always grants good fortune. (140)
Longevity, health, sovereignty, and the increase of sons and grandsons [are attained];
even a woman or a widow who recites it unintentionally shall obtain liberation. 141.
A woman who desires it shall obtain freedom from widowhood in another birth;
she destroys all suffering, fear, and obstacles, and removes the affliction of misfortune. 142.
It pacifies all afflictions and bestows dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
whatever desire one contemplates, that one certainly attains. 143.

She is the wish-fulfilling cow for what is desired, the celestial wish-granting tree for every imagination, and the thought-gem for whatever is thought of—she who brings about all auspiciousness. 144.
One who desires liberation should recite it constantly and shall attain the glory of liberation;
indeed, for one who desires enjoyment, its recitation bestows the fruit of their desires. 145.
O Goddess, for one capable of recitation, the solar, the Gāṇapatya, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Śaiva [mantras] grant success; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. ||146||
Now, O lady of beautiful countenance, I shall describe the locations for the recitation performed for specific desires:
either at the ocean, or on the bank of a river, or in the abode of Hari and Hara. (147)
In a temple of Śakti, in a cow-pen, in an auspicious temple of all the gods, at a banyan tree or at the root of a dhātrī tree, or likewise in a monastery or in Vṛndāvana; ||148||
In a pure and stainless place, or even through constant practice, one should perform this recitation with freedom from worldly desire and in silence. (149)
They attain success in a cremation ground, in a place of terror, likewise at the foot of a banyan tree, at the root of a dhautara tree, or in the vicinity of a mango tree. 150.
It is better for the guru’s son to be a fool; for him, all auspicious rites, initiations, vows, and ascetic practices will succeed, but not otherwise. 151.
For the sake of destroying the impurities of saṃsāra and for the cessation of the bonds of existence, the knower of reality always performs the bath in the waters of the Guru-gītā. (152)
And that very Guru is himself directly the eternal, ever-present, supreme knower of Brahman;
all his places are undoubtedly sacred. 153.
He is entirely pure and holy, abiding in his own nature;
indeed, all the hosts of gods dwell there in that field and sacred seat (pīṭha). 154.
Whether seated or lying down, walking or standing, even while speaking;
whether mounted on a horse or an elephant, asleep or even awake—(one should recite it). 155.
And the pure one who is always wise, by means of the chanting of the Guru-gītā, finds that through the mere sight of him, rebirth no longer exists. ||156||
Just as water is in the ocean, milk in milk, and ghee in ghee, and just as space remains when a jar is broken, so does the Self abide within the Supreme Self. 157.
In the same way, the wise living self is absorbed into the Supreme Self;
the wise one rejoices in unity there, day and night. 158.
O Guru, all those who are satisfied with you are liberated; of this there is no doubt.
Enjoyment and liberation are theirs, and Sarasvatī dwells upon the tip of their tongues.
Such is the great liberated one who always abides as a wise man;
he for whom [the world] performs devotion with all effort toward his inner state (bhāva). ||159||
O Pārvatī, one becomes free from all doubt and liberated; both worldly enjoyment and liberation belong to him, and Sarasvatī resides upon the tip of his tongue. 160.
By this recitation of the Guru-gītā, all living beings attain every perfection, as well as worldly enjoyment and liberation; of this there is no doubt. (161)
Truth, truth, and again truth—this Dharma and Sāṃkhya have been proclaimed by me.
There is nothing equal to the Guru-gītā; this is the truth, the absolute truth, O fair-faced one. 162.
O scorcher of foes, there is but one God, one Dharma, and one ultimate goal;
there is nothing higher than the guru, nor is there any reality superior to the guru. 163.
Blessed is the mother, blessed is the father, blessed is the lineage and likewise the family;
blessed is the goddess Earth, for devotion to one's guru is very difficult to attain. 164.
O Goddess, there is no doubt that the body, the senses, the vital breath, wealth, one's own kin and relatives, mother, father, family, and even the preceptor are all [dependent on it]. (165)
O Goddess, all the acts of recitation, vows, and ascetic penance performed through ten million births until the end of the kalpa become fruitful solely through the satisfaction of the Guru. (166)
"O fair-faced one, it is the truth, the absolute truth, that those men who are unfortunate do not serve their gurus, even though they possess the power of knowledge and austerity. (167)
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśa, as well as the celestial sages, the ancestors, the kinnaras, the siddhas, cāraṇas, yakṣas, and other sages and people. ||168||
For those who are contented and well-pleased indeed become devoted to their guru;
just as water poured at the root nourishes the fruits and flowers.
The state of being a guru is the supreme sacred ford; any other sacred ford is useless.
O Goddess, the big toe of the foot serves as the refuge for all sacred fords. 169.
Through recitation one attains victory and shall obtain infinite fruit;
abandoning all inferior actions and lowly states of existence. (170)

The Ugradhyāna, situated in the Kukkuṭa [mudrā], bestows the fruits of inferior actions; likewise, the Gurugītā should be recited during departure, in battle, or in the midst of danger from enemies. ||171||
By reciting it, one attains victory; at the time of death, it bestows liberation.
And every rite performed by the son of the Guru succeeds everywhere. 172.
This secret, which has been told by me before you, must not be spoken;
it must be guarded with great effort, for you are dear to me. 173.
O Pārvatī, I tell you the truth, the absolute truth: one must not even mention in one's mind the names of Śiva, Brahmā, Gaṇeśa, Viṣṇu, and the others. 174.
O Goddess, this must be spoken to one whose mind is thoroughly matured and who is endowed with faith and devotion; for you, my beloved, are always my very self. 175.
The *Gurugītā* should never be spoken, even in one's mind, to one who is unrighteous, deceitful, fraudulent, heretical, or an atheist. (176)
There are many gurus who seize the wealth of their disciples;
rare, O Goddess, is this guru who removes the suffering of his disciples.
The sole mantra for being rescued from the ocean of saṃsāra, the perfected mantra worshipped by the gods beginning with Brahmā and by the sages.
I pay homage to the mantra of the King of Gurus, which destroys poverty, suffering, fear, and sorrow, and which removes all great terrors.
Thus ends the *Gurugītā* within the *Uttarakhaṇḍa* of the glorious *Skandapurāṇa*, in the dialogue between Īśvara and Pārvatī.
May this be an offering to the venerable Guru Dattātreya.
